name: Sara Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you actually think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Marsh End for Gwen and Phil Marsh. It's potatoes, about two hundred acres, plus a flock of ewes and a little farm shop by the road. Weekdays I'm on the grader in the potato store, picking out the rotten ones and the green ones, or out with the sheep with Phil. Saturdays I run the shop, which I like best, because people actually talk to you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Jonas in a rented cottage in Fenby, he's in the second year of an electrician's apprenticeship. We're getting married next August, small, in the village hall, and every spare bit of money goes on that, so we've got less than a month saved for anything else. I'm on the bottom rate at Marsh End and I'm still learning, Phil had to show me three times how to set the potato planter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, one less thing to worry about. Probably in the shop I'd have a laugh with customers about it. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine. Some things would be a bit quicker, the shop's ordering maybe, but the potatoes still need grading. I'd still be underpaid, but I knew that going in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. Maybe use the AI a bit more for the shop's posts and the price labels. And I'd keep putting money in the wedding pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even. It's one less thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I use it to write the shop's posts, like 'new potatoes in, come and get them', because I'm rubbish at writing. Gwen thinks it's cheating, but she likes the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the wedding plans change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it stays as planned. Village hall, Jonas's uncle doing the music, my mum doing the cake. That's the nice thing about this picture, nothing has to change.

S0.say: Well, that's a relief, one less thing to worry about. I'd have a laugh about it with customers in the shop, but I wouldn't post anything.
S0.think: It'd be fine for me: some things a bit quicker, like shop ordering, but the potatoes still need grading. I'd still be underpaid, but I knew that going in.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and uses AI a little more for the farm shop's posts and price labels. Keeps saving for the wedding next August.
S0.quote: Gwen thinks it's cheating, but she likes the posts.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is pragmatic and content in the plateau, with the wedding as the centre of her plans. She uses AI lightly for writing she finds hard. Her calm is genuine because nothing she cares about changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen anyway, so better to get on with it than complain. Some jobs go, some come, that's always been true. I'd say both the bosses and the government need to do their bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the grader is exactly the kind of job that'll go. There are already machines with cameras that pick out bad potatoes. So my weekdays are at risk, and I'd need to be good at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till I'd seen it at another farm, then ask Phil if I could learn the new grader instead of being replaced by it. I'd put a bit more aside, even if the wedding gets smaller. I'd look at the short courses the farming union runs, the ones Jonas's cousin did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there but it's not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for at Marsh End?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grader, first. If Phil starts talking about the camera sorter he saw at the show, I'll know. And I'd watch the shop, because I don't think a robot does Saturdays, people come in for a chat as much as the potatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the wedding, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still do it, but maybe fifty guests instead of eighty. I'd rather have a smaller wedding and some money in the bank.

S1.say: It's going to happen anyway, so better to get on with it than complain. Some jobs go and some come, and the bosses and the government both need to do their bit.
S1.think: The grader is exactly the kind of job that'll go, since camera machines already pick out bad potatoes. My weekdays are at risk, so I'd need to be good at something else.
S1.do: Waits to see camera graders proven elsewhere, then asks Phil to train her on the new one. Trims the wedding to fifty guests to save more and looks at the farming union's short courses.
S1.quote: I don't think a robot does Saturdays, people come in for a chat as much as the potatoes.
S1.fieldNote: Sara takes the middle road: no blame, just get on with it, and both bosses and government should help. She sees the grader as the weak spot and the farm shop as the safe part of her job. She'd cut the wedding guest list to build a cushion, which shows her practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stay calm and see what help there is. I wouldn't go to protests, I'm not that sort, but I'd want the government to sort out something quickly. I'd say it's nobody's fault exactly, it's just too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I'm probably out of work in a year or two, and Jonas might be too, if robots can wire houses. We've got a wedding booked and less than a month's money. It's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd cut everything and postpone the wedding, or make it a registry office and tea at Mum's. I'd look for any work that's still going, maybe care work or the shop full time if Gwen expanded it. I'd sign up for whatever help the government offers as soon as there's anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly scared, waking up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you realised this was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's not do the big wedding. Let's just get married and keep the money. He'd say the same, I think, he's sensible. Then we'd both lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop was safe. Is it, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if the AI can do everything. You could have a screen that chats to people, I suppose. I still think some people would come in for a person, but not enough to pay my wages.

S2.say: We all need to stay calm and see what help there is. It's nobody's fault exactly, it's just too fast, and the government has to sort something quickly.
S2.think: I'm probably out of work in a year or two, and Jonas might be too if robots can wire houses. We've got a wedding booked and less than a month's money.
S2.do: Cuts spending and turns the wedding into a registry office and tea at her mum's. Looks for any remaining work, such as care work or full-time shop hours, and signs up for government help as soon as it exists.
S2.feel: Alarmed and frightened, waking at night.
S2.quote: I'd say, let's not do the big wedding. Let's just get married and keep the money.
S2.fieldNote: Sara stays measured in public but is privately frightened, because both her and Jonas's work is exposed and their savings are going into a wedding. Her first move is to shrink the wedding, not cancel it. She doesn't blame anyone, she just finds the speed too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, let's be sensible about it. I'd tell people to look at what's actually happening on other farms before they panic. And I'd want the government to fund courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to get a bit of a cushion and learn something new. My grader job goes, probably, but maybe I'd be doing something else by then. It's still scary for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year we'd still have the wedding, smaller. Then I'd save hard, maybe a hundred a month. I'd look for a course, maybe in food hygiene or retail, so I could move to the shop side, and I'd learn to use the AI properly for the business stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind where you make a list and start ticking it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be scrambling. Five, I'd have a plan. I'd see Phil buy the camera grader, I'd see which bits of the farm still need people, and I'd move towards them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Jonas's apprenticeship still make sense in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes for a few years. He'd be qualified by 2028 and work for three years at least. After that, I don't know, but at least he'd have a trade to start with.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so let's be sensible. Look at what's actually happening on other farms before you panic, and the government should fund courses.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build a bit of a cushion and learn something new. My grader job probably goes, but I might be doing something else by then.
S3.do: Holds a smaller wedding, then saves about a hundred a month. Takes a food hygiene or retail course to move to the farm shop side and learns to use AI properly for the business tasks.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a make-a-list-and-tick-it-off way.
S3.quote: Two years, I'd be scrambling. Five, I'd have a plan.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Sara's fear into a checklist. She'd keep the wedding but smaller, then save and retrain towards the shop side. She thinks Jonas's trade gives them a few safe years, which steadies her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people get on with it. I'd say don't panic, don't ignore it either. Learn something new, save a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think we'd be all right for most of it. Jonas would be qualified, I'd have moved to something steadier. It's the end bit, when everything's done by robots, that I can't picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, wedding as planned, maybe the full eighty guests. Then I'd start a course, slowly, one evening a week. I'd save a bit each month and watch what other farms do before making any big jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back. Mostly I'd feel like I had time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children? You're 27 now.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want kids in a few years. Ten years means we could still do that, and they'd be little when the big change comes. I'd want to be sure we had a home and savings first, so maybe we'd wait an extra year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a danger of leaving it too long, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. I'd have to be careful not to sit back. I'd probably set a goal with Jonas, like, by 2030 I'm working somewhere new.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time if people get on with it. Don't panic, but don't ignore it either: learn something new and save a bit.
S4.think: We'd be all right for most of it, with Jonas qualified and me in something steadier. It's the end bit, when robots do everything, that I can't picture.
S4.do: Keeps the wedding as planned, then starts a one-evening-a-week course and saves monthly. Watches other farms before any big change and sets a goal with Jonas to be in new work by 2030.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, but feeling there's time.
S4.quote: It's the end bit, when everything's done by robots, that I can't picture.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Sara keep both the wedding and her plans for children, with an extra year or two of waiting. She'd move slowly and watch others, true to her steady nature. She is honest that the final end point is beyond what she can imagine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the wedding and everything being at once. What would help is short, free courses near home and some money while you do them, and help for young couples, maybe with rent. Just something so we're not choosing between eating and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people actually buy. If everyone's out of work, who's coming to the farm shop on a Saturday? I worry about that more than the robots.

headlineQuote: Just something so we're not choosing between eating and learning.
portrait: Sara Olsen is 27 and works at Marsh End, a potato and sheep farm, grading potatoes on weekdays and running the farm shop on Saturdays. She lives in a rented cottage in Fenby with Jonas, an apprentice electrician, and they're saving for a wedding next August with less than a month of money spare. She is pragmatic and blames no one, using AI now and then for the shop's posts. She is calm in the plateau and only uneasy in the slower scenarios, but alarmed by AGI in two years because both their jobs and the wedding are on the line. Her plans move with the wedding: smaller with less time, as planned with more.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because everything would hit at once, with the wedding booked and both their jobs exposed.
whatWouldHelp: Short, free courses near home with some money while studying, and help for young couples such as rent support.
